messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Amira

Amira was sixty-eight when her daughter called from the hospital. It was a Thursday morning in late spring, and Amira had just finished dressing the Hendersons' two youngest children for school—a routine she had performed five mornings a week for nearly twelve years. The call came as she was wiping jam from a toddler's chin. Her daughter Layla had been walking home from her shift at the clinic where she worked as a nurse, cutting through the park near her apartment as she always did. A man had emerged from behind the trees. What happened next—the struggle, the knife, the way Layla's screams had brought a jogger running—would fracture Amira's sense of safety in a way that no amount of time seemed able to mend.

In those first weeks after the attack, Amira had moved through the Hendersons' house like a ghost. She fed their children, braided their hair, sang to them at naptime, but something essential had withdrawn. The police had arrested a man three days after the assault, but he had been released on bail pending trial. Amira had come to believe with absolute certainty that he was still out there, that the system had failed her daughter, that the people responsible for this failure—the judge, the bail bondsman, the lawyers—would face nothing at all for what they had allowed to happen. This conviction had taken root and would not budge, no matter how many times Layla or her husband tried to reassure her.

The park where Layla had been attacked was less than two miles from the Hendersons' home. Amira had stopped driving that direction entirely. What had once been her quickest route to the grocery store, the pharmacy, the mosque where she had prayed for forty years, became impossible. She would take the long way around, adding twenty minutes to simple errands, and even then her hands would grip the steering wheel so tightly that her knuckles turned white. The park itself—she could not go there. She had not walked through it since Layla was a girl. Now the very thought of driving past its entrance made her chest tighten.

In the months that followed, Amira's world had contracted in other ways. When she was at the Hendersons' house, she found herself watching the children's father with an intensity that surprised her. She noticed the way he stood, the tone of his voice when he spoke to his wife, the angle of his shoulders as he moved through rooms. She was not afraid of him exactly, but she could not stop monitoring him, could not stop searching his face and his gestures for signs of something dangerous lurking beneath. At the grocery store, she watched other shoppers—men especially, but not only men. She watched how they looked at people, where their hands were, whether they moved too close to anyone. Walking from her car to the store entrance, she found herself glancing behind her repeatedly, her neck tense, her breath shallow. Someone might be following her. It seemed important to check.

At home, she had begun to suppress any thought of Layla's attack the moment it surfaced. When an image would start to form—Layla's face, the park, the man's silhouette—Amira would push it away forcefully, redirecting her mind to the children's schedules, to recipes, to anything else. But the effort of this constant mental pushing had left her exhausted. She agreed to things she did not want to do, said yes to plans she dreaded, simply because saying no required energy she did not have. Her husband had invited his brother to stay for two weeks; Amira had wanted to refuse, but the thought of the conflict, the explanation, the risk of disappointing him, had made her simply nod and smile.

It was her youngest grandson, now ten years old, who had finally prompted her to seek help. He had asked why Grandmother never came to the park anymore, why she looked so worried all the time. In his simple question, Amira had seen herself clearly: a woman living in fear, unable to protect the people she loved most, unable to stop watching for danger that might never come. She had made an appointment with a therapist, hoping that someone could help her understand why Layla's trauma had become her own, and why she could not seem to stop believing that she had failed.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Age discrepancy: Patient is 71, but vignette states Amira was sixty-eight: The vignette describes Amira as 'sixty-eight when her daughter called from the hospital,' which contradicts the patient demographic of age 71. This is a factual inconsistency in the demographics check.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Amira was seventy-one when her daughter called from the hospital. It was a Thursday morning in late spring, and Amira had just finished dressing the Hendersons' two youngest children for school—a routine she had performed five mornings a week for nearly twelve years. The call came as she was wiping jam from a toddler's chin. Her daughter Layla had been walking home from her shift at the clinic where she worked as a nurse, cutting through the park near her apartment as she always did. She fed their children, braided their hair, sang to them at naptime, but something essential had withdrawn. The police had arrested a man three days after the assault, but he had been released on bail pending trial. Amira had come to believe with absolute certainty that he was still out there, that the system had failed her daughter, that the people responsible for this failure—the judge, the bail bondsman, the lawyers—would face nothing at all for what they had allowed to happen. This conviction had taken root and would not budge, no matter how many times Layla or her husband tried to reassure her. She was certain that danger was everywhere, that it could emerge at any moment from any direction, and that her vigilance was the only thing standing between her loved ones and catastrophe. The thought of Layla being attacked again consumed her; she imagined it happening to herself, to her grandchildren, to strangers on the street. These images came unbidden and felt impossibly real, as though they were happening in the present moment rather than in her mind.

The park where Layla had been attacked was less than two miles from the Hendersons' home. Amira had stopped driving that direction entirely. What had once been her quickest route to the grocery store, the pharmacy, the mosque where she had prayed for forty years, became impossible. She would take the long way around, adding twenty minutes to simple errands, and even then her hands would grip the steering wheel so tightly that her knuckles turned white. The park itself—she could not go there. She had not walked through it since Layla was a girl. Now the very thought of driving past its entrance made her chest tighten, her breathing shallow and rapid, her heart pounding so hard she thought it might break through her ribs. When she did force herself to drive the main road, she found herself gripping the door handle, bracing as if for impact. At night, she lay awake replaying the details of the assault—details Layla had shared only once, in the hospital—and her mind would construct scenarios of what might have happened if the jogger had not appeared, if Layla had fought back differently, if Amira herself had insisted her daughter take a different route home that evening. She had come to believe, in the darkest hours, that she bore some responsibility for not having prevented what she could not possibly have prevented.

In the months that followed, Amira's world had contracted in other ways. When she was at the Hendersons' house, she found herself watching the children's father with an intensity that surprised her. She noticed the way he stood, the tone of his voice when he spoke to his wife, the angle of his shoulders as he moved through rooms. She was not afraid of him exactly, but she could not stop monitoring him, could not stop searching his face and his gestures for signs of something dangerous lurking beneath. At the grocery store, she watched other shoppers—men especially, but not only men. She watched how they looked at people, where their hands were, whether they moved too close to anyone. Walking from her car to the store entrance, she found herself glancing behind her repeatedly, her neck tense, her breath shallow. Someone might be following her. It seemed important to check. She had also begun to suppress any thought of Layla's attack the moment it surfaced. When an image would start to form—Layla's face, the park, the man's silhouette—Amira would push it away forcefully, redirecting her mind to the children's schedules, to recipes, to anything else. But the effort of this constant mental pushing had left her exhausted. She agreed to things she did not want to do, said yes to plans she dreaded, simply because saying no required energy she did not have. Her husband had invited his brother to stay for two weeks; Amira had wanted to refuse, but the thought of the conflict, the explanation, the risk of disappointing him, had made her simply nod and smile.

It was her youngest grandson, now ten years old, who had finally prompted her to seek help. He had asked why Grandmother never came to the park anymore, why she looked so worried all the time, why she kept checking the windows. In his simple question, Amira had seen herself clearly: a woman living in fear, unable to protect the people she loved most, unable to stop watching for danger that might never come. She had made an appointment with a therapist, hoping that someone could help her understand why Layla's trauma had become her own, and why she could not seem to stop believing that she had failed her daughter, that the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that her constant vigilance was the only thing keeping her family alive.
